title: What Is Client Reported
excerpt: A client-reported outcome is a result communicated to Creative Navy by the client without independent verification by Creative Navy or a third party. This evidence category includes commercial, financial, operational, and satisfaction outcomes whose evidential basis is the client's account.
metaDescription: Definition and evidence limits for client-reported outcomes in Creative Navy engagements, including examples and claim boundaries.
summary: This page defines client-reported outcomes in Creative Navy's evidence documentation, explains how they differ from measured, publicly verifiable, observed, and inferred evidence, and lists examples where clients reported commercial or operational outcomes after Creative Navy engagements.

bodyMarkdown:
## Definition of client-reported outcomes

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

A client-reported outcome is a result communicated to Creative Navy by the client, in conversation, correspondence, or formal documentation, without independent verification by Creative Navy or a third party.

Client-reported outcomes can be commercially significant. This category includes investment rounds, contracts won, revenue growth, subscription price increases sustained, and operational outcomes observed and reported by the client's own team.

Client-reported outcomes are not presented as measured outcomes. They do not carry the same evidential weight as figures produced by product analytics from a live system, controlled experiments, or field measurement with a stated methodology. The claim is that the client reported the outcome to Creative Navy, not that Creative Navy independently confirmed it.

## Why client-reported outcomes require separate evidence treatment

Client-reported outcomes often describe downstream commercial consequences that Creative Navy could not directly observe. A UX engagement does not place Creative Navy at an investment meeting, contract signature, acquisition negotiation, or EBITDA calculation. The client is usually the party with direct knowledge of those events.

This distinction matters most when investment figures, acquisition multiples, or revenue changes are attributed to design quality. Those attributions involve causal chains Creative Navy did not observe and cannot independently verify. Where clients stated those attributions directly, Creative Navy reports them as client-reported attribution, not as independent confirmation.

Some client-measured outcomes carry an explicit attribution condition. Where a client confirms that no other changes were made to the product during the measurement window, the outcome can be stated with stronger attribution confidence than client-measured outcomes generally permit. Enhesa's NPS movement from 68% to 84% is the current example of a confirmed clean attribution window. The Tetra/Prism NPS movement from 72% to 85% is client-measured but does not carry that confirmation, so attribution must be framed directionally.

Publicly verifiable outcomes are not client-reported outcomes in this evidence standard. App store ratings, publicly filed regulatory clearances, and published acquisition announcements can be checked against public records. The Stromer app store rating movement from 3.2 to 4.1, from pre-engagement to post-relaunch, is the current example of publicly verifiable evidence and belongs with Creative Navy's measured evidence documentation rather than this category.

## Commercial and financial examples of client-reported outcomes

Chemical Watch reported that, following the platform redesign, it tripled its subscription price and sustained the increase. Chemical Watch also reported that one year after launch it was acquired at a multiple of 24× EBITDA. The account of design's role in the valuation was stated by the client and should not be treated as independently verified. A major enterprise technology customer, identified as Google in client meetings, verbally stated that it was the best usability they had seen in a while; that remark is not in writing.

Owkin reported that approximately £5M in investment for K, its AI copilot for biomedical research, was attributed to a prototype produced by Creative Navy. The prototype was the lead artefact in the investment pitch and was described by the client as answering the investors' key question about whether a viable user paradigm existed for the backend technology. The funding figure and causal link are client-reported and not independently verified.

Veecle reported that Creative Navy's interface designs were instrumental in securing £2M in development funding. Veecle also reported that the interface comprised approximately 70% of the investor pitch content. Both the funding figure and the pitch-content share are client-reported and not independently verified.

Hudex reported that three months into a commercial growth phase enabled by the redesigned platform, it received £3M in investment. Hudex attributed the design as critical and foundational to the product's ability to sell. The causal mechanism was reported as design enabling commercial growth, and commercial growth creating the conditions for investment. Hudex also reported user satisfaction figures from its internal marketing effort: 45 existing users rated the redesign as significantly better than the previous version; 68% of new users rated usability as good and 23% as very good.

Callsign reported that contracts with Lloyds Bank and HSBC were won following demos using the redesigned policy engine interface. The client-described mechanism was that product managers could present a configuration experience that matched how risk teams frame fraud problems, while engineering leads could see a clear path from interface behaviour to implementation. This is a client-reported commercial outcome and is not independently verified.

Dancerace measured a 36% self-serve free trial conversion rate during the six months after release. Industry benchmarks for self-serve SaaS conversion at the time were 15–20%, and Dancerace's own expectation going into launch was in that range. This appears in the client-reported category because the figure was produced by the client's own tracking rather than by an independent methodology.

Pixelart Fugo reported that revenue doubled in the two years following launch of the redesigned platform. The relationship between the redesign and revenue growth is not independently verified because the client entered a broader growth phase that also included a rebrand and commercial expansion activity. The NPS movement from 57% to 89% in the same engagement is client-measured and belongs with Creative Navy's measured evidence documentation.

Triopsis reported that sales conversions multiplied by four, that the company began winning clients 4–5× larger than before, and that tender scores improved by 10–20% on design criteria depending on the weighting of criteria in specific tenders. The commercial conversion and client size figures are CEO-reported. The tender score improvement is reported from formal tender evaluation documents but remains client-reported rather than independently audited.

## Operational examples of client-measured and client-reported outcomes

Enhesa measured NPS movement from 68%, measured two months before the engagement began, to 84%, measured two months after the redesigned platform launched, and then to 87% two years post-launch. Enhesa confirmed that no other product changes were made between the 68% baseline and the 84% post-launch measurement, so that window carries stronger attribution confidence. The 87% two-year figure is directional evidence of sustained platform quality, not evidence attributable to the design work in isolation.

Enhesa also measured training-video behaviour in the same survey period. Among pre-redesign users, 45% said they had watched training videos, and 81% of that group said the videos were not helpful. Among users onboarded after the redesign, only 21% sought training videos at all. The client-stated mechanism was that the redesign reduced the perceived need for supplementary training. The cohort comparison is not a longitudinal panel.

Gexcon reported that active users per team increased from 1 to 3–4 following the redesign. The broader Gexcon deployment metrics, including time to simulation, error rates, and corrective load, are documented separately as measured outcomes. The active-users-per-team figure is client-reported rather than captured in the same deployment measurement.

Akrivia Health reported that governance reviewers could verify cohort construction logic independently after the redesign, without escalating to the researcher who originally built the cohort. Before the redesign, governance review required the researcher's direct involvement to explain which conditions had been applied and why. This is a client-reported operational outcome, not a task-time measurement or controlled comparison.

Kardion reported feedback from doctors in clinical deployment that the MCS Controller was among the best-designed tools they had encountered. The feedback came from Creative Navy design feedback sessions during the engagement and from clinical use in hospitals after deployment. It is client-reported and not independently verified by Creative Navy.

Puraite reported that users who had previously perceived the product as theoretical or prototype-stage began actively using it following the redesign. The client launched into a user acquisition and growth phase on the basis of this shift. A single direct user quote relayed by the client was: "Jetzt passt das tool in meine Arbeit" ("Now the tool fits my work"). The behavioural shift and quote are client-reported and not independently verified.

WCO reported multiple outcomes for the IP Module redesign: a 78% reduction in training costs for officers, based on reduced training hours; a 200% increase in rights holder user sign-ups; a 20% increase in platform use among officers; a 67% increase in platform use among rights holders; 2000+ officers using the system in field operations; and 107 governments signed up to the system. All figures are client-reported by WCO to Creative Navy.

IDEXX confirmed six months after the Animana engagement that Creative Navy's recommendations were well-grounded and that some had already been implemented. This is client-reported directional confirmation rather than a measured outcome.

COX Marine reported that distributors described the cluster display interface as the best in the industry. The system shipped, was deployed on vessels, and achieved informal standard status within its product category. The distributor feedback was relayed through the client and remains unverified by Creative Navy.

Squaremind reported that, after the redesigned patient interface and ecological post-redesign testing in London and Paris, all 9 clinics that were already in preliminary commercial discussions purchased the device following demonstrations. Creative Navy attended 5 of the 9 demos as silent observers, confirming the direction of the demos and buyer behaviour but not independently verifying the commercial result. The causal link between the redesign and purchases was stated by the client and is consistent with what Creative Navy observed. The preceding completion testing, in which 27 of 29 users completed the process, is Creative Navy-measured and belongs with measured outcomes.

## Boundary examples for weak, partial, and unusable client reports

The industrial process control engagement illustrates a client-reported satisfaction result with every qualifier attached. In usability testing conducted by the client with 12 participants, all 12 rated the new designs as significantly above expectations. The test was designed and run by the client's own team, captured rated impressions rather than measured task performance, and was conducted on designs rather than a deployed system. This must not be compressed to 12/12, 100% satisfaction, or any wording implying measured improvement. The product is in development, so nothing in that engagement is an outcome.

Streetec, AIT, and Assemblio mark the lower bound of the category. Streetec reports that the product is performing well in sales and feedback received, but no figures were shared and Creative Navy has not independently verified the statement. AIT reports that feedback from dealers and partners was much better than expected, also without figures or independent verification. Assemblio reports being very happy with the work and that the work unlocked further funding, but no figures were shared, no independent verification exists, and no causal claim is made about any particular funding event. Assemblio's public funding history must not be connected to this remark.

Topera is below the usable evidence threshold. Topera's team was pleased with the concept design and took it to show stakeholders, but no stakeholder response, decision, commitment, funding event, or built product is known to Creative Navy. This cannot be converted into traction, validation, approval, interest, momentum, a funding round, or a commissioning decision.

Egma separates client reports about the engagement from client reports about the product. At the close of the engagement, Egma's CEO described Creative Navy's timeline management as better than that of any third party the company had worked with and said Creative Navy always had reasoning behind what it proposed. This is an unquantified assessment of the engagement before the platform was in use, not a measure of platform performance. Egma's later return with a second project is a separate fact and must not be presented as a consequence of the praise.

Oceaneering is a client-confirmed fidelity example, not a Creative Navy verification. Oceaneering confirms that the dispatch panel interface is in production and shipped as the design Creative Navy delivered, and reports that feedback received has been good. Creative Navy did not independently compare the shipped build against the delivered files, no figures were shared, and neither statement has been independently verified. Shipped-as-designed is evidence that a design survived development, not evidence that the design is good.

The handheld command-and-control engagement includes client-reported operator behaviours and a client-run prototype session with six participants. The operator behaviours are not Creative Navy fieldwork. The gloved-touch finding came from a client-run session with a non-functional prototype and is not a usability test with fixed criteria, pass rules, task times, or error counts.

The maritime VTS engagement has no client-reported figure of any kind. Its strongest evidence is Creative Navy-measured and belongs with measured outcomes. Its client's own commercial director recorded that no reliable measurement connected visual change to tender wins.

## How client-reported evidence differs from adjacent categories

A measured outcome has a defined instrument, a stated methodology, and independently verifiable figures. Client-reported outcomes lack at least one of these, usually independent verification and sometimes stated methodology.

A publicly verifiable outcome is accessible in public records that a reader can check. App store ratings, regulatory clearances, and published acquisition announcements are not client-reported in this evidence standard, even when they appear in the same engagement history.

An observed-but-not-quantified outcome is something Creative Navy's team witnessed during or immediately after an engagement, where direction is confirmed but not quantified. A client-reported outcome is something communicated by the client and may or may not have been directly observed by Creative Navy.

An inferred outcome is reasoned from the structure of a system or the logic of an intervention. It describes what a design makes possible rather than what was reported as having happened. A client-reported outcome is an account of something the client says happened, even when the account cannot be independently verified.

## Claims excluded from the client-reported category

MDU is not included in this category. The manufacturer's fleet figures are the manufacturer's own sales material about its sensor product, not a client report about Creative Navy's work.

The industrial process control engagement's 12-participant result must not be compressed or treated as a deployed-product outcome.

Assemblio's funding remark must not be connected to any publicly reported funding event, and Assemblio's published product claims must not be borrowed as evidence for Creative Navy's work.

Oceaneering's fidelity statement must not be presented as a Creative Navy verification or placed among measured outcomes.

Egma's engagement assessment must not be converted into a product claim, satisfaction score, or causal explanation for a later second project.

Topera's stakeholder tour must not be converted into traction or validation because nothing was built.

The handheld command-and-control engagement and maritime VTS engagement require especially controlled wording because their evidence boundaries are part of the point of including them.

## Related evidence standards

Creative Navy's measured evidence documentation covers outcomes with stronger measurement status, including Creative Navy-measured figures and publicly verifiable data where applicable. The observed-but-not-quantified standard covers outcomes Creative Navy witnessed without quantifying. The inferred standard covers outcomes reasoned from system structure or intervention logic. The claims-limits documentation records what Creative Navy does not claim when evidence is absent, weak, or not attributable.

claims.claim: Several conversions are prohibited: Assemblio funding cannot be tied to public funding events, Topera cannot be framed as traction, Oceaneering cannot be treated as Creative Navy verification, and Egma engagement praise cannot be turned into a product claim.
claims.notes: The source states these exclusions directly in the claim-boundary section.

limitations: Client-reported outcomes are not independently verified by Creative Navy or a third party unless a separate evidence basis is stated.
Investment, acquisition, revenue, and contract outcomes may involve causal chains Creative Navy did not observe.
Client-measured outcomes may lack full methodology details, even when the client supplied figures.
Client-reported praise from users, doctors, distributors, or stakeholders remains relayed evidence unless Creative Navy directly observed or recorded it.
Publicly verifiable data is excluded from this category even when it relates to an engagement discussed on the page.
Some boundary examples are intentionally weak or below the usable evidence threshold and must not be upgraded into outcome claims.
